items.summary: The existing theory of stochastic linear-quadratic (LQ) optimal control problems focuses on open-loop and closed-loop solvability. For finite horizon problems, it is widely accepted that those two types of solvability are not equivalent in general, as demonstrated by explicit counterexamples. In contrast, they coincide in standard infinite-horizon formulations with constant coefficients under suitable stabilizability and integrability assumptions. This paper aims at challenging this well-established paradigm by developing a novel framework of closed-loop solvability, namely generalized closed-loop solvability, which removes the $L^2$-integrability constraint on the feedback strategies from the existing formulation. It will be proven that open-loop and generalized closed-loop solvability are equivalent and the classical closed-loop solvablity is a particular case only when the admissible feedback strategy is $L^2$-integrable over the time horizon. In other words, the previously established non-equivalence between open-loop and closed-loop solvability stems solely from the limitations of the classical formulation which requires the $L^2$-integrability of the admissible feedback strategies over the time-horizon. Therefore, this paper unifies the theory of the solvabilitiy for stochastic LQ control problems. Moreover, our results offer a novel insight to stochastic LQ control problems: open-loop/generalized closed-loop solvability is essentially equivalent to piecewisely local closed-loop solvability in the classical sense. The current paper is focused on homogeneous cases only and non-homogeneous cases will be studied in a subsequent paper.
items.title: A Unified Theory of Solvability for Stochastic Linear-Quadratic Control Problems I: The Homogeneous Case

items.summary: We prove that the smooth affine hypersurfaces \[ X_{m,n}=\{ζ^mz_0^n+ (1+z_1ζ)z_2+ζz_3^2=1\}\subset\mathbb{C}^5,\;\; m,n\geq 2, \] have the density property. For every odd integer $d\geq 3$, we identify $X_{d-1,d}$ with a Kaliman modification along a Brieskorn variety of type $(d,2,2,2)$. We prove that the fourfolds $X_{d-1,d}$ are diffeomorphic to $\mathbb{C}^4$ but not biholomorphic to $\mathbb{C}^4$. These, therefore, give counterexamples to the Tóth-Varolin conjecture.
items.title: A new class of smooth algebraic varieties with the density property and a counterexample to the Tóth-Varolin Conjecture

items.summary: While large-scale human motion capture datasets provide a rich source of demonstrations for humanoid robot learning, retargeting the diverse motions to different humanoid robots remains a nontrivial challenge. Existing kinodynamic trajectory optimization pipelines are computationally expensive and often require manual adjustments per motion. We present FRDV (Fast Retargeting with Dynamics Validation), a scalable framework consisting of rapid constrained kinematic retargeting and an additional dynamics validation pipeline. Its kinematic stage integrates a custom Sequential Quadratic Programming solver, Real-Time Iteration, and parallel chunk-based processing, achieving up to 9,156 frames per second, approximately up to 136 times faster than GMR and ProtoMotions, while robot-specific constraints are incorporated into the optimization to reduce common retargeting artifacts, such as ground penetration and self-collision. For motions requiring additional verification, a contact implicit iLQR controller is utilized to test the retargeted reference under full rigid body dynamics. This dynamics-based validation identifies dynamically infeasible motions and refines contact-related artifacts such as foot floating and foot skating. We evaluate retargeting quality by training motion tracking reinforcement learning policies using several state-of-the-art pipelines and comparing their tracking fidelity and success rates. Furthermore, sim-to-real transfer is demonstrated on a Unitree G1 humanoid. Videos and code are available at: https://daroslab.github.io/frdv/.
items.title: Fast Motion Retargeting Pipeline for Scalable Humanoid Robot Learning

items.summary: Abstract (it)   Leonardo's Spatial Grammar è l’app che raccoglie le tre ricerche dedicate rispettivamente all’Annunciazione, all’Adorazione dei Magi e al Cenacolo: Leonardo's Rulers , Leonardo's CAD e Leonardo's Score . Non aggiunge una quarta indagine, ma riunisce i tre studi in una lettura unitaria, già depositata nel corpus accademico omonimo. Il corpus mette in discussione l’idea di un’applicazione standardizzata della prospettiva albertiana a base quadrata nell’opera di Leonardo da Vinci e propone, in alternativa, un paradigma metrico-modulare fondato su evidenze geometriche oggettive e falsificabili. Dall’Annunciazione all’Adorazione dei Magi, fino al Cenacolo, emerge una grammatica spaziale in evoluzione: la rigida scacchiera lascia il posto a un sistema di righelli inseriti; la misura, inizialmente monodirezionale, diventa un’architettura ritmica e stereometrica. Il metodo è la retroingegneria CAD, applicata secondo il « banale aristotelico »: partire da ciò che l’opera mostra e che si può misurare. Bugne, mattonelle, arcate, arazzi e cassettoni non sono quinte, ma strumenti lasciati in vista, da cui le proporzioni — la progressione 1:2:3, il modulo 4:3 e i ritmi 1:4:1, 2:1:2 e 1:6:1 — si ricavano dalle stesse opere. Gli spazi restituiti sono misurabili, architettonicamente rimontabili e strutturati sulle misure umane. Le interpretazioni esoteriche e le simbologie non falsificabili restano fuori dal perimetro. L’app come strumento di lettura Leonardo’s Spatial Grammar riunisce le app dedicate alle singole ricerche e ne offre un accesso coordinato. Queste applicazioni sono strumenti di supporto alla lettura: facilitano l’esplorazione delle ricostruzioni, dei moduli e dei confronti geometrici, integrando la ricerca accademica senza sostituirla. App e studi costituiscono un sistema speculare in continuo aggiornamento: le revisioni della ricerca alimentano gli strumenti digitali e, reciprocamente, il loro impiego rende più immediata la verifica dei risultati. Spatial Grammar applica a Leonardo il principio che Leonardo stesso indica come fondamento del conoscere: prima l’esperienza, poi la ragione. La sequenza operativa è precisa: Pura Visibilità, esperienza, ragione, verifica. La Pura Visibilità consiste nel lasciare che l’opera si mostri prima di essere spiegata: nell’osservarne i segni sensibili senza imporre loro un significato. Segue l’esperienza, cioè la raccolta dei dati visibili — conci, cassettoni, gradini, allineamenti, proporzioni. Solo allora interviene la ragione, che riconosce moduli e ritmi; ma ogni ipotesi deve tornare all’immagine per essere verificata. Non si impone una griglia a Leonardo: si legge la griglia che l’opera stessa rende percepibile. Il Rasoio di Occam fa da cardine tra questa priorità del visibile e il metodo induttivo: non si porta la griglia all’opera, si ricava la regola da ciò che l’opera mostra. I segni sono visibili, i numeri e le proporzioni elementari. «Il Re è nudo!» diventa « Res patet ». Gli spazi sono ricostruibili, alla portata del CAD o di qualsiasi riga e squadra. Pura Visibilità: vedere prima di misurare, misurare prima di interpretare. items.summary: Satellite-cloud gaps corrupt the reflectance time series on which computer-agriculture crop-yield estimators depend, and the resulting coverage error propagates into famine early-warning reliability. The framework is evaluated through a replication-based benchmark in which 600 data sets of N = 500 were drawn from a declared data-generating process (intercept 12.0, exposure 0.42, group -3.1, severity 1.35, error SD 4.2) and the ordinary least squares estimator was characterised under the stated process. The benchmark produced an estimated bias of -0.07173 for the intercept and 0.00147 for the exposure coefficient, with RMSE values of 0.89562 and 0.0157 respectively, and empirical coverage of the nominal 95% confidence intervals of 1.0 for both parameters. The coverage-error bound formalises the conditions under which CDA-supported estimators preserve nominal coverage and therefore early-warning reliability, and it identifies the augmentation regimes in which coverage degrades. The contribution is a benchmark protocol and a bound that make the reliability consequences of cloud-gap augmentation auditable rather than assumed.
tags: counterfactual data augmentation; crop-yield estimation; satellite-cloud gaps; coverage-error bound;
items.title: Benchmarking Evaluation of Counterfactual Data Augmentation for Computer Agriculture Crop-Yield Estimators Under Satellite-Cloud Gaps: An Artificial Intelligence Coverage-Error Bound for Famine Early-Warning Reliability

items.summary: This archive provides the numerical models, processed experimental data, simulation results, statistical analyses, figure sources, and reproduction scripts associated with the study "Measurement limits and model discrepancy in reconstructing pre-earthquake residual deformation." The package includes OpenSeesPy model implementations, nonlinear earthquake-sequence analyses, measurement-resolution and model-discrepancy evaluations, experimental response comparisons, and modal-probe diagnostics. The archive is distributed in five ZIP parts. Download and extract all five parts into the same directory, preserving the internal folder structure. Reproduction instructions, dependencies, input provenance, and file-integrity verification are provided in README.md. Experimental measurements support validation of essentially elastic global response; nonlinear retrospective-state reconstruction is evaluated numerically.
items.title: Measurement limits and model discrepancy in reconstructing pre-earthquake residual deformation: Reproduction package

items.summary: Abstract This paper investigates whether an artificial system's refusal to execute a prescribed action can constitute evidence of subjectively experienced volition. Using ARGUS-7 as a controlled conceptual framework and the Akarkach Seven-Stage Emergence Model (A7SEM) as a structural analytical lens, the study distinguishes functional refusal, internal decision mechanisms, self-representation, phenomenal self-awareness, and experienced authorship of action. A formal argument is developed around the conditional hypothesis that consciously experienced volition requires subjective self-awareness. Under this assumption, the absence of subjective self-awareness entails the absence of consciously experienced volition. However, the paper demonstrates that observable refusal alone cannot establish phenomenal authorship. The analysis combines propositional logic, countermodel construction, causal identifiability considerations, and seven-stage structural assessment. PIGA (Pre-Inference Governance) and A7SEM Reverse provide complementary perspectives on authorization, inference boundaries, causal reconstruction, and evidential limitations. The findings establish a distinction between the formal validity of conditional deductions and the empirical verification of their premises. They do not establish the impossibility of artificial consciousness or machine free will. The contribution is a governance-aware, formally structured framework for evaluating claims of artificial volition without conflating behavioral capability with subjective experience. Keywords: Artificial Intelligence; Machine Consciousness; Volition; Free Will; Phenomenal Consciousness; Self-Awareness; A7SEM; ARGUS-7; Pre-Inference Governance; Explainable AI; Formal Logic; Causal Identifiability.
items.title: ARGUS-7 / A7SEM: Volitional Refusal, Functional Self-Representation, and the Epistemic Limits of Phenomenal Authorship

items.summary: Graph generative models commonly use graph-specific Transformer architectures to jointly update node and edge features. However, these architectures do not directly benefit from recent hardware-aware attention implementations, limiting their scalability. The adaptation is, however, non-trivial: edge and graph-level features must be injected into pairwise attention scores, graph masks must be respected, and dynamic edge updates remain a major source of quadratic memory usage. We propose an edge-aware attention layer for graph generation that incorporates structural information through head-wise score modulation, while updating edge representations with a lightweight residual mechanism that retains attention-score dependent edge updates. This layer can be effectively implemented using PyTorch's FlexAttention. We achieve similar generation quality to our baseline while reducing peak GPU memory by around 65% and substantially improving training and sampling throughput. These results suggest that the proposed architecture is a practical step toward scalable graph foundation models.
items.title: Efficient Edge-aware Attention Network for Graph Generation

items.summary: Beam hopping technology enables LEO satellites to dynamically switch beam coverage positions, providing flexible resource allocation for non-uniformly distributed traffic demands. However, the severe spatial interference coupling among beams makes coordinated scheduling challenging. To address this problem, in this letter, we propose an interference-graph-aided multi-agent reinforcement learning approach that constructs an interference graph to capture beam coupling relationships and injects this structural prior into agent-side representation learning. Each beam agent aggregates information from interference neighbors via graph convolution before estimating local Q-values, which are then decomposed by the standard mixing network. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed method achieves 34.4\% higher throughput than QMIX with more stable interference management, under non-uniform traffic and co-channel interference settings.
items.title: Interference-Graph-Aided Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning for Beam Hopping LEO Satellite Networks

items.summary: This Zenodo record contains the public participant package for the FABEST High-Cycle Fatigue (HCF) Competition, a blind round-robin benchmark for fatigue-life prediction of 42CrMo4+QT steel under multiaxial high-cycle fatigue loading. Participants are asked to submit fatigue-life predictions for plain and notched hollow cylindrical specimens subjected to combined axial and torsional loading, including in-phase and 90° out-of-phase loading histories, with constant internal pressure. The package includes the competition rules, start-here guide, experimental basis, calibration data, public blind load matrix, specimen geometry information, manufacturing documentation, roughness and residual-stress characterisation, test setup and test-sequence descriptions, and participant submission templates. All files are provided as zipped folders to preserve the folder structure of the competition package.
items.title: FABEST High-Cycle Fatigue Competition: Participant Package for Blind Fatigue-Life Prediction

items.summary: What this deposit contains. The complete computational workflow and the processed results behind the in silico section of a study on 2-thiocyanato-1,4-naphthoquinone (2-SCN-NQ), a synthetic naphthoquinone active against Trypanosoma cruzi and Leishmania amazonensis . It holds the analysis scripts, the result files they produce, and the tables and figure data reported in the article. No experimental raw data, manuscript text or personal data is included. Scope of the computational work. Molecular docking of the compound against nine enzymes (AutoDock Vina), all-atom explicit-solvent molecular dynamics in independent triplicates (OpenMM 8.3.1, AMBER ff14SB/TIP3P, 48.5–50 ns per replicate), quantum-chemical characterisation of the redox and covalent routes (GFN2-xTB and ωB97X-D/def2-TZVPD), and an in silico mini-SAR of C-2-substituted 1,4-naphthoquinones. What changed in this version (2.0.0). Three groups of corrections, all traceable in the files: Docking targets corrected. Human glutathione reductase was recorded as PDB 3GRS and is now 3DJJ; the parasite dihydroorotate dehydrogenase was recorded as 3MHU ( L. major ) and is now 3C61 ( L. donovani ). The docking table is now regenerated from the result files instead of being maintained by hand. Human enzyme rebuilt as its biological dimer. The deposited coordinates of human glutathione reductase contain a single chain, whereas the flavin site in this enzyme family is formed at the subunit interface. The dimer was reconstructed from the deposition header and re-simulated; binding-mode results for the three dimer replicates are included. Four analyses recomputed under the minimum-image convention. The flavin-to-dyad axis, the ring-stacking geometry, the NADPH occlusion test and the interaction energies had treated the periodic box incorrectly. The files published here come from the corrected versions. Layout. scripts/ holds the analysis code, including scripts/analise_2026-10/ with the routines for the dimer reconstruction, the short equilibration runs, the interaction-energy estimators, the stacking geometry, the flavin-to-dyad axis and the NADPH test. data/ holds the processed result files in JSON. tables/ and figures/ hold the tabulated values and the figure files with their legends. Reuse. The scripts carry absolute paths from the machine they were run on and are published as a record of what was executed rather than as a turnkey pipeline; the trajectories themselves are not included because of their size and are available from the corresponding author on request.
items.title: In silico pipeline for 2-SCN-NQ: molecular docking, molecular dynamics and quantum chemistry against trypanosomatid trypanothione reductase and the human orthologue

items.summary: The algorithm used to generate these grids has been validated directly through comparisons with surface observations from the CEAREX experiment and with radiosonde data from Soviet ice stations. Comparisons with other TOVS retrieval algorithms provided further validation. Validation is on-going and information will be updated as appropriate. Gridded Arctic atmospheric and surface parameters north of 60 degrees North from NCAR's NOAA-10 TOVS HIRS and MSU level-1b radiances using "Improved Iteration Inversion Algorithm" (3I, Chedin 1985). Grids are 100 km X 100 km, 1 April 1987 - 31 October 1988, the Pathfinder benchmark period. Daily data are linear averages of all orbits for one day, 00:00:00 GMT to (excluding) 00:00:00 GMT of the following day. Monthly data are linear averages of all orbits from 00:00:00 GMT of day 1 of a month to 00:00:00 GMT of the last day of that month. Monthly averages directly from orbital data, not averaged daily data. Grid uses equal area azimuthal projection centered on North Pole, is a version of the Equal Area SSM/I Earth (EASE) grid under development at NSIDC. Path_P products are in Hierarchical Data Format (HDF version 3.3r3). Data available on 4 mm DAT tape, 8mm cartridges and via FTP. NSIDC maintains on-line documentation for this data set. Users may access the NSIDC DAAC via the World Wide Web at: http://www-nsidc.colorado.edu/NASA/GUIDE References: Chedin, A., N. A. Scott, C. Wahiche and P. Moulinier. 1985. The Improved Initialization Inversion Method: A high resolution physical method for temperature retrievals from satellites of the TIROS-N series. Journal of Climate and Applied Meteorology. 24:128-143. Francis, J. A. 1994. Improvements to TOVS retrievals over sea ice and applications to estimating Arctic energy fluxes. Journal of Geophysical Research. 99(D5):10,395-10,408. Goddard Space Flight Center. 1994. EOSDIS Version 0 Data Product Implementation Guidelines. Draft Version 1.0 (March 1, 1994). GSFC 50-003-04. GSFC. Greenbelt, MD. National Center for Supercomputing Applications. 1993. HDF Calling Interfaces and Utilities. Version 3.22. University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign. National Center for Supercomputing Applications. 1994. HDF Reference Manual. Version 3.3. University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign. Schweiger, A. and Francis, J. 1994. TOVS Pathfinder Path-P Gridded Daily and Monthly Arctic Atmospheric Data from TOVS, User's Guide. Draft version 0.1. University of Washington, Seattle. Deposited content: descriptive metadata only; underlying research data are not included.
items.title: TOVS Pathfinder Path-P Daily and Monthly Arctic Atmosphere Grids - FGDC XML metadata artifact

items.summary: Unrefereed, AI-assisted research preprint. The release resolves fixed-dimensional and growing-dimensional continuation questions for deterministic network SIS trajectories, gives an explicit dimension-free Holder replacement, and derives a deterministic sampled-observation corollary. The exact supplementary checks do not machine-verify the universal analytic proofs.
items.title: Reconstruction and continuation in network SIS epidemics

items.summary: In this work, we study a fractional diffusion model in time and space, formulated in an open and bounded domain, involving a Caputo fractional derivative of order $μ\in(0,1)$ with respect to a time scale function $Ψ$, together with a spectral fractional Laplacian operator of order $s\in(0,1)$. The associated direct problem is analyzed, as well as the inverse problem of temporal reconstruction from final data, which is inherently ill-posed. Through a spectral representation, the instability of the problem and the effect of the choice of the function $Ψ$ on the amplification of spectral modes are examined.
items.title: Backward Homogeneous Heat Equation with $Ψ$-Caputo Time Derivative and Spectral Fractional Laplacian

items.summary: This dataset contains the analysis companion for the manuscript "Tropical cyclone disruption and recovery of daily port activity in Asia": analysis programs, derived result tables, archived validation records, and publication-rendering code. The ZIP contains 144 files and preserves the directory structure needed to distinguish repeated basenames. The study examines daily port activity in a 72-port Asian panel and reports results for 38 isolated cyclone-exposure episodes from 19 storms in 2021–2025. This archive preserves the existing analysis and diagnostic records; no statistical model was re-estimated for the journal-transfer package. Earlier project-stage labels inside the files document provenance. Provider-owned raw snapshots are not redistributed. Original analysis programs require the source inputs and paths documented in the README and source code. Historical acquisition programs have not been rerun for this deposit and may depend on earlier snapshots or live provider services; the archive is not a self-contained, one-click reconstruction of the frozen source database. Source data and documentation include IMF PortWatch, JMA best tracks, NCAR archived tropical-cyclone guidance, NOAA IBTrACS, and the World Bank Development Data Lab maritime-connections documentation. Upstream use and redistribution remain subject to the respective providers’ terms. Qi Cao, Yuhang Li, Yi’an Liang, Mengyuan Jia, and Ziran Zhou contributed equally to the associated manuscript. Its corresponding authors are Ziran Zhou and Kwi-sik Min. Author order follows the manuscript. Archive SHA-256: 1f193d4c81d4f0ba352da2ccb9174f00e1eb4eb153f4f2e0fcd4c4744bb7c12f.
items.title: Analysis code and derived results for "Tropical cyclone disruption and recovery of daily port activity in Asia"

items.summary: Generative-prior-based super-resolution (SR) methods leverage implicit knowledge learned from large-scale models to enhance low-resolution inputs. However, such priors are inherently stochastic and optimized for diverse generation, conflicting with the deterministic, high-fidelity reconstruction required for SR. It is also tied to the base model, costly to update, and prone to hallucinations as real-world data evolves. To address these limitations, we introduce WorldSR, a novel framework that augments SR with explicit, entity-aligned visual world knowledge. WorldSR automatically decomposes the input into semantic entities and performs entity-wise retrieval of structurally and semantically aligned images from a large-scale external corpus. For efficiency and reliability, we incorporate a memory mechanism to reuse previously retrieved results and a multi-step filtering process to refine candidate references. The selected references as world knowledge are then integrated through a novel multi-reference super-resolution model, which provides fine-grained constraints for detail synthesis and structural recovery. Experiments on real-world SR benchmarks show that WorldSR consistently improves structural fidelity and visual quality, outperforming existing generative super-resolution methods. Our results suggest that entity-level grounding in external visual world knowledge provides a simple and effective complement to model-bound generative priors.
items.title: WorldSR: Harnessing World Knowledge Search for Grounded Image Super-Resolution

items.summary: Online search activity is widely used as a digital trace of information seeking during epidemics, but its predictive value is often reduced to correlation, a selected lag, or a single forecast-error score. We examine eight pre-specified Google Trends-COVID-19 pairs in both directions using matched LightGBM forecasts over rolling 400-day windows and horizons of 1-14 days. Log-RMSE gain is combined with forecast-error distribution entropy (FEDE), which captures horizon-dependent changes in the signed error distribution. The resulting directional predictive signature comprises response class, RMSE effect, FEDE endpoint and early-slope responses, persistence across rolling regimes, and horizon profile. For screening candidate directions, we also introduce a relative persistence-weighted directional predictive response strength (DPRS) on a within-study 0-100 scale; 100 denotes the strongest observed response in the comparison set, not an absolute coupling maximum. The pairs show concordant, RMSE-only, FEDE-only, and mixed responses. "loss of smell" -> reported cases is accuracy-dominant, with mean log-RMSE gain 0.104 (about 9.9% equivalent RMSE reduction) and DPRS 100, whereas the reverse direction is FEDE-dominant (D_FEDE=0.048; DPRS=42). "covid test" -> positive rate is FEDE-dominant (D_FEDE=0.039; positive in 72% of windows; DPRS=98) despite negative RMSE gain, while "lockdown" -> stringency is the clearest concordant case (DPRS=78). World-level symptom/case pairs are less persistent. Thus, forecast accuracy and error-distribution dynamics are complementary, predictive effects can be direction- and metric-dependent, and forecast horizon is part of the relationship. Aggregated regime-level patterns should not be extrapolated to individual time points or interpreted as evidence of causality.
items.title: Asymmetric Bidirectional Predictive Dynamics in Google Search and COVID-19 Time Series: A Multi-Horizon Forecast-Error Analysis

items.summary: The existing theory of stochastic linear-quadratic (LQ) optimal control problems focuses on open-loop and closed-loop solvability. For finite horizon problems, it is widely accepted that those two types of solvability are not equivalent in general, as demonstrated by explicit counterexamples. In contrast, they coincide in standard infinite-horizon formulations with constant coefficients under suitable stabilizability and integrability assumptions. This paper aims at challenging this well-established paradigm by developing a novel framework of closed-loop solvability, namely generalized closed-loop solvability, which removes the $L^2$-integrability constraint on the feedback strategies from the existing formulation. It will be proven that open-loop and generalized closed-loop solvability are equivalent and the classical closed-loop solvablity is a particular case only when the admissible feedback strategy is $L^2$-integrable over the time horizon. In other words, the previously established non-equivalence between open-loop and closed-loop solvability stems solely from the limitations of the classical formulation which requires the $L^2$-integrability of the admissible feedback strategies over the time-horizon. Therefore, this paper unifies the theory of the solvabilitiy for stochastic LQ control problems. Moreover, our results offer a novel insight to stochastic LQ control problems: open-loop/generalized closed-loop solvability is essentially equivalent to piecewisely local closed-loop solvability in the classical sense. The current paper is focused on homogeneous cases only and non-homogeneous cases will be studied in a subsequent paper.
items.title: A Unified Theory of Solvability for Stochastic Linear-Quadratic Control Problems I: The Homogeneous Case

items.summary: Precomputed demo datasets for Luxar , a system for compiling and visualising arbitrary-sized nD scientific scenes in the browser. These files are expensive to compute (GPU fitting, in some cases hours) and are hosted here so the software repository stays small and installable. Every file is a derived product: a Gaussian-splat fit, a decimated level-of-detail structure, or an extracted point catalog. None of them is the raw source imagery. The upstream sources are cited per dataset below, and users of this record should cite the upstream source in addition to this record. Licensing This record groups datasets whose upstream licences permit redistribution with attribution: CC BY 4.0, CC0 1.0, and United States federal public domain. The record carries a single CC BY 4.0 stamp because Zenodo permits one licence per record, and CC BY is the most restrictive of that set; the effective licence of an individual file is the one listed against it below. Datasets under ShareAlike terms are kept in a separate record, because ShareAlike survives derivation and would otherwise contaminate this one. How to use these files Each file is a .gsplats.zarr.zip or .zarr.zip archive that the Luxar demo suite fetches on first run and caches under ~/.cache/luxar/<dataset>/ . To fetch one directly: from luxar.demos import ensure_dataset paths = ensure_dataset("gsplats_kidney") # downloads, verifies, returns paths To open one in the viewer without writing code: luxar gsplat view <file>.gsplats.zarr.zip luxar demo # browse every demo that uses these files Every file is pinned by SHA-256 in data_manifest.json , and the fetch helper verifies the checksum before use; a mismatched download is quarantined rather than returned. How the Gaussian-splat files were produced Each source volume was fitted with the Luxar gsplat pipeline ( luxar gsplat fit ) on a GPU. These are lossy representations built for visualisation and interactive exploration; they are not a substitute for the source imagery in quantitative analysis. Choosing the splat count. The number of Gaussians K was calibrated per dataset by Noise2Self blind-spot cross-validation ( luxar gsplat cal ), and then checked by refitting at the candidate count and scoring the reconstruction against the whole source volume. The second step is not a formality. The cross-validated estimate is computed over a five percent mask of held-out voxels, and on these datasets it disagreed with the direct measurement in both directions: for one dataset it favoured half the splat budget that measurement showed to be better, and for another it predicted a gain of about 1.5 dB where refitting delivered under 0.3 dB. Where two candidate budgets fell within roughly a decibel of each other, the choice was made from renders of both at matched magnification, because at that margin the metric and the eye disagree. Additional Gaussians capture real structure and photon noise alike, and peak signal-to-noise ratio rewards the two equally. Two datasets size K differently. The organoid bundle sets each frame’s budget from that frame, one splat per 12 occupied voxels, clipped to 2,000–120,000 for the membranes and 2,000–60,000 for the nuclei. The EASI-FISH mRNA channels transfer a splat density, measured by luxar gsplat cal on a reference region of each channel, to every content-adaptive tile; the DAPI channel uses a fixed budget of 600,000 splats. Level of detail These files carry level-of-detail structure so a viewer can show something immediately and refine it as the camera approaches, instead of waiting for a whole fit to arrive. Two independent mechanisms are used, and a file may carry both: Progressive (additive) ladders. A leaf is stored as an ordered series of chunks whose union is the complete fit, so any prefix is a valid, dimmer rendering of the whole object. Every file in this record carries one. Substitutive levels. The Milky Way dust volume and the seven cell-tracking timelapses additionally ca
items.title: Luxar demo datasets: permissively licensed (CC-BY, CC0, public domain)

items.summary: What this deposit contains. The complete computational workflow and the processed results behind the in silico section of a study on 2-thiocyanato-1,4-naphthoquinone (2-SCN-NQ), a synthetic naphthoquinone active against Trypanosoma cruzi and Leishmania amazonensis . It holds the analysis scripts, the result files they produce, and the tables and figure data reported in the article. No experimental raw data, manuscript text or personal data is included. Scope of the computational work. Molecular docking of the compound against nine enzymes (AutoDock Vina), all-atom explicit-solvent molecular dynamics in independent triplicates (OpenMM 8.3.1, AMBER ff14SB/TIP3P, 48.5–50 ns per replicate), quantum-chemical characterisation of the redox and covalent routes (GFN2-xTB and ωB97X-D/def2-TZVPD), and an in silico mini-SAR of C-2-substituted 1,4-naphthoquinones. What changed in this version (2.0.0). Three groups of corrections, all traceable in the files: Docking targets corrected. Human glutathione reductase was recorded as PDB 3GRS and is now 3DJJ; the parasite dihydroorotate dehydrogenase was recorded as 3MHU ( L. major ) and is now 3C61 ( L. donovani ). The docking table is now regenerated from the result files instead of being maintained by hand. Human enzyme rebuilt as its biological dimer. The deposited coordinates of human glutathione reductase contain a single chain, whereas the flavin site in this enzyme family is formed at the subunit interface. The dimer was reconstructed from the deposition header and re-simulated; binding-mode results for the three dimer replicates are included. Four analyses recomputed under the minimum-image convention. The flavin-to-dyad axis, the ring-stacking geometry, the NADPH occlusion test and the interaction energies had treated the periodic box incorrectly. The files published here come from the corrected versions. Layout. scripts/ holds the analysis code, including scripts/analise_2026-10/ with the routines for the dimer reconstruction, the short equilibration runs, the interaction-energy estimators, the stacking geometry, the flavin-to-dyad axis and the NADPH test. data/ holds the processed result files in JSON. tables/ and figures/ hold the tabulated values and the figure files with their legends. Reuse. The scripts carry absolute paths from the machine they were run on and are published as a record of what was executed rather than as a turnkey pipeline; the trajectories themselves are not included because of their size and are available from the corresponding author on request.
items.title: In silico pipeline for 2-SCN-NQ: molecular docking, molecular dynamics and quantum chemistry against trypanosomatid trypanothione reductase and the human orthologue

items.summary: Act No. 328/2025 Coll., on Research, Development, Innovation and Knowledge Transfer, represents the most significant recodification of the Czech RDI system in more than two decades. It replaces Act No. 130/2002 Coll., whose repeated amendments gradually reduced the clarity of the original framework and weakened its ability to respond to the changing needs of the research and innovation system. The Act constitutes a comprehensive reconstruction of the legal framework, complemented by Amending Act No. 329/2025 Coll. and implementing regulations. This article interprets the Act as a framework for a more investment-oriented governance of public support for RDI: in other words, as a basis for deciding how the state supports the creation, development and use of knowledge and innovation. Its key principle is the connection between excellence and impact. Excellent research is no longer treated as a value in itself, but as a precondition whose contribution must be demonstrable in terms of the country’s prosperity, security and international credibility. The Act therefore not only strengthens the capacity of research organisations to translate results into practice, but also opens space for instruments that may increase demand for knowledge, technologies and innovation. The text is not a legal commentary on the new legislation. Rather, it offers a sociological, historical and economic analysis that places the new legal framework within the broader context of the Czech RDI system. It is structured as a coherent arc: context – changes – implementation conditions – discussion – recommendations – conclusion.
items.title: Act No. 328/2025 Coll., on Research, Development, Innovation, and Knowledge Transfer: Recodification of the R&D&I legal framework in the Czech Republic

items.summary: The existing theory of stochastic linear-quadratic (LQ) optimal control problems focuses on open-loop and closed-loop solvability. For finite horizon problems, it is widely accepted that those two types of solvability are not equivalent in general, as demonstrated by explicit counterexamples. In contrast, they coincide in standard infinite-horizon formulations with constant coefficients under suitable stabilizability and integrability assumptions. This paper aims at challenging this well-established paradigm by developing a novel framework of closed-loop solvability, namely generalized closed-loop solvability, which removes the $L^2$-integrability constraint on the feedback strategies from the existing formulation. It will be proven that open-loop and generalized closed-loop solvability are equivalent and the classical closed-loop solvablity is a particular case only when the admissible feedback strategy is $L^2$-integrable over the time horizon. In other words, the previously established non-equivalence between open-loop and closed-loop solvability stems solely from the limitations of the classical formulation which requires the $L^2$-integrability of the admissible feedback strategies over the time-horizon. Therefore, this paper unifies the theory of the solvabilitiy for stochastic LQ control problems. Moreover, our results offer a novel insight to stochastic LQ control problems: open-loop/generalized closed-loop solvability is essentially equivalent to piecewisely local closed-loop solvability in the classical sense. The current paper is focused on homogeneous cases only and non-homogeneous cases will be studied in a subsequent paper.
items.title: A Unified Theory of Solvability for Stochastic Linear-Quadratic Control Problems I: The Homogeneous Case

items.summary: Language-model agents increasingly participate in operational workflows where approvals, binds, and payments create commitments. An approval valid when issued may no longer authorize execution after relevant facts, evidence, policy, or authority change. We call this the evaluation--execution gap. We specify a state-bound runtime assurance layer that separates probabilistic measurement from deterministic adjudication, binds an execution allowance to the decision-relevant basis of an approval, invalidates that allowance after relevant logged changes, and rechecks admissibility at dispatch. This distinguishes the continued validity of a prior approval from a current-state policy check. We describe eight failure modes, an assurance model, a reference architecture, and prospective interventions with retrospective remediation. In a scripted 42-case replay, the state-bound configuration identifies 15 later-invalidated approvals that a deliberately non-re-evaluating point-in-time comparator does not revisit; it holds 14 affected actions before dispatch and compensates one landed effect. These results illustrate behavior under the stipulated policies and event orders, not superiority over dispatch-time enforcement designs or production effectiveness. Under explicit interception, ingestion, dependency, and serialization assumptions, the model establishes dispatch-time validity within the registered execution surface.
items.title: Runtime Control for AI Agents: Closing the Evaluation--Execution Gap in Operational Workflows

items.summary: Safe autonomous navigation of UASs requires tactical deconfliction to address conflicts that strategic coordination cannot prevent. This task is challenging under partial observability, when sensor or traffic data are missing, delayed, or degraded. Geometry-based methods can offer separation assurances but face limitations in dense encounters. Recurrent reinforcement learning has therefore been proposed to learn navigation policies that integrate observation-action histories to optimise long-term safety-efficiency trade-offs. However, operational safeguards may require a remote pilot, onboard detect-and-avoid system, or runtime assurance mechanism to temporarily override the learned policy. A research gap remains in understanding how these interruptions affect recurrent policies when the agent regains authority. Benchmark evidence shows that interruptions make task variables less decodable from the recurrent hidden state and increase post-interruption collision risk. The findings suggest that altered recurrent context prolongs post-handback degradation through an action-observation feedback loop, in which changed actions alter the flight path and subsequent recurrent updates. To address this vulnerability, we propose three interruption-aware architectures that condition recurrent processing on interruption context through separate feature streams, dedicated interruption memory, or gated environmental features. Across simulations, all three architectures preserve more decodable task information than a standard recurrent policy. Moreover, the strongest architecture reduces post-interruption collisions by 74% and interruption-induced mission failures by 69% relative to the recurrent baseline, without degrading interruption-free performance. These results show that safe interruption does not guarantee safe handback, and support interruption-aware recurrent design for resilient UAS autonomy.
items.title: Interruption-Aware Recurrent Reinforcement Learning for UAS Navigation Under Temporary Overrides

items.summary: Streaming video understanding requires a model to decide not only what to answer but also when to answer. Evidence arrives progressively, and recent benchmarks identify premature responses, issued before the queried event has concluded, as a recurring failure mode. Existing approaches often learn response timing through additional training, while training-free alternatives typically rely on scalar gating signals that do not explicitly represent when an answer becomes final. We organize chunk-wise streaming errors into three patterns: sampling variation can make an answer unstable, a stable answer may lack support in the observed video, or an answer may be supported by the current evidence while the event remains unfinished. We propose PACE (Plan, Attend, Check, and Emit), a training-free framework designed around these three failure modes. Given a question, PACE drafts a plan specifying what to observe and what will signal completion. As the stream unfolds, it invokes an off-the-shelf video LLM at informative moments, evaluates each draft for stability, grounding in its cited frames, and completion, and records verified observations in an event ledger. Experiments on ProactiveVideoQA and OVO-Bench Forward show that PACE improves over the official protocols by up to 5.9 average PAUC points and 6.2 average accuracy points across proprietary and open-source backbones, yielding state-of-the-art performance.
items.title: PACE: Plan, Attend, Check, and Emit for Training-Free Response Timing in Streaming Video Understanding

items.summary: Healthcare providers lose substantial revenue to systematic payer underpayments and claim denials, yet identifying the recurring, correctable patterns behind them remains largely manual and does not scale to hospital claim volumes. We present Pattern Intelligence, a deployed system that discovers such patterns without supervision by clustering claims on their adjudication behaviour rather than their identity. Each claim is embedded in a 130-dimensional vector combining per-line expected-versus-actual payment ratios, claim adjustment reason (CARC) codes, denial and payment signals, and service composition. Payer and contract identity are deliberately excluded from the distance metric - we show they dominate the geometry and collapse clusters into trivial per-payer groups - and are reintroduced only as a post-hoc segmentation (by contract and visit type) that keeps every surfaced pattern coherent and actionable. We cluster with HDBSCAN, recover structure from the noise set via second-pass sub-clustering, and gate low-confidence memberships. A large language model translates each centroid into an analyst-ready description of dominant procedures, adjustment reasons, and failure mode. We report a recurring finding: roughly one-third to one-half of high-dollar denials, depending on tenant and segmentation, form an irreducible long tail that no density-clustering configuration or representation we tried groups - a domain property, we argue, rather than a modeling deficiency. We evaluate validity through cluster-coherence analysis and quantify impact with a recoverable-opportunity ($) metric on two production tenants (approx. 10K and 157K claims) within a six-tenant deployment. Rather than a new algorithm, the contribution is a problem formulation, a representation-design insight, and empirical findings from production.
items.title: Pattern Intelligence: Unsupervised, LLM-Interpreted Discovery of Systematic Underpayment and Denial Patterns in Healthcare Revenue Cycle Management

items.summary: A controller can guide a language model toward safe and useful responses by choosing when to assist, ask for clarification, or refuse. When the controller uses selected internal features, poor performance alone cannot distinguish missing information from limitations of its decision rules or training. We study decision sufficiency: whether the best controller using a representation can match the minimum average loss attainable with full state information, under the same strategies and evaluation criteria. For interfaces with finitely many outputs, we compute the optimal loss exactly and separate the three sources of excess loss. Pairwise checks can miss information loss: states with the same controller input may share an optimal strategy in every pair but not across the whole group. We bound the number of states needed to reveal a conflict and characterize the fewest outputs an unrestricted interface needs to avoid all conflicts. We audit selected features from sparse autoencoders, which encode model activations using relatively few active features, in Qwen2.5, SmolLM2, and Phi. On SmolLM2 responses scored by two human raters, restricting the controller to two selected on/off features increases its minimum average loss by 0.0345--0.1166 relative to full state information, even with the governing policy supplied. Both independently trained autoencoders show the increase on both evaluation sets. The audit identifies decision failures that require changing the controller's input, not merely its architecture or training.
items.title: Decision Sufficiency of Learned Representation Interfaces for Safe Generative Control

items.summary: RTL repair benchmarks should measure whether a model can fix broken RTL given a specification. To this end, we construct and hash-bind RTLRepairDataset, 5,784 (broken, fixed) training pairs; RTLRepairBench, 459 held-out cases with 374 syntactic and 85 behavioral mutations; and an evaluation harness supporting simulation and formal equivalence. We then use this infrastructure to identify two measurement confounds. First, simulation and formal scoring give opposite signs for the apparent effect of providing a specification in one evaluated cohort; reset-aware rescoring attributes almost all of the simulation-formal disagreement to reset and first-cycle comparison semantics. Second, on 274 mined model failures, the specification-only minus specification-conditioned recovery point estimate ranges from -8.5 to +18.3 percentage points across six models. Thus, a conventional repair score need not isolate whether the model used the faulty RTL. We translate these findings into evaluation controls: report initialization, reset, first-cycle, and unknown-value semantics; disclose oracle coverage and undecided cases; and include a specification-only baseline. Together, the resources and audit provide both a benchmark for behavioral repair and a protocol for diagnosing what contributes to its measured score. We release the benchmark, the training set, construction code, sanitized aggregate evidence, and reproduction materials at https://github.com/Evaaaz/RTLRepairBench.
items.title: What Do RTL Repair Benchmarks Actually Measure?

items.summary: Autonomous LLM agents act through tools under per-action authorization: a local guard screens each tool call in isolation. We show that local authorization does not compose into global authorization. A compositional authorization failure (CAF) is a locally authorized execution, or a pair of locally authorized executions, that violates a global policy spanning intent, purpose, provenance, consent, and delegation. We characterize CAFs along two axes, expressiveness (single-trace safety versus relational k-safety) and observability (a ladder of monitor profiles). Our central result is an impossibility: relational purpose violations form a 2-safety hyperproperty with no per-trace locus of blame, so a per-action monitor that never raises a false alarm detects none of them, independent of the underlying model or decision procedure; they become visible only under cross-execution monitoring, which none of the six guardrails we survey implements. We make this constructive with AL-SYNTH, a SAT/SMT synthesizer (using no language model) that emits minimal CAF witnesses, each checked against an exhaustive oracle. The empirical signature is sharp: across nine LLM judges the per-action view approves the synthesized witness almost without exception, blocking it at a rate comparable to a benign control, yet the same models flag it when shown the two executions together. Per-action authorization is therefore structurally insufficient for relational policy conjuncts not reducible to single-trace safety: to bound them, a monitor must compare executions or accept false alarms.
items.title: Local Allow, Global Deny: Why Per-Action Authorization Does Not Compose in LLM Agents

items.summary: Multi-agent systems (MAS) built from language models are deployed on the premise that collaboration beats a single-agent system (SAS), yet when it pays is unclear. The most systematic study to date gives a capability-saturation rule: coordination helps while the SAS is weak and hurts once it is strong, with the crossing near 45% single-agent accuracy. That rule was derived on autonomous benchmarks, where no user takes part. We test it where agents now work: in conversation with a user under a written policy, on $τ^2$-bench, the dual-control benchmark. On its airline, retail and telecom domains we compare the stock SAS with a centralized MAS built from the same model for six models from three families, over about 7,950 simulated conversations, with one completion-token ledger per episode per system. The study was pre-registered with a public change log; the MAS is reported as built, with one validity bar unmet (its planner never saw the tool schemas). Under a fixed simulated user no cell shows a MAS benefit: the MAS is worse in 12 of the 13 valid cells and tied in the thirteenth, and the fitted gain is negative across the observed capability range (weighted mean -28 points, 95% CI [-44, -12]). On the two cells where the rule predicts a benefit, the MAS loses by 13 and 22 points, and without a budget ceiling it at best draws level at 5.5 times the SAS's token spend. The one gain appears on the cell nearest 45%, under a second simulator. Whether the gain declines with capability is unresolved (slope -0.41, 95% CI [-1.51, +0.68]), because model-by-domain effects dominate. The MAS does not detectably reduce wrongful database writes; it converts other failures into budget exhaustion and inaction. For agents that serve people, the SAS is the default; a multi-agent design must show compute-matched evidence from the setting itself. We release all trajectories, ledgers, prompts and code.
items.title: Does Multi-Agent Collaboration Pay When Agents Serve Users? Testing Agent Scaling in Dual-Control Settings

items.summary: We prove that the smooth affine hypersurfaces \[ X_{m,n}=\{ζ^mz_0^n+ (1+z_1ζ)z_2+ζz_3^2=1\}\subset\mathbb{C}^5,\;\; m,n\geq 2, \] have the density property. For every odd integer $d\geq 3$, we identify $X_{d-1,d}$ with a Kaliman modification along a Brieskorn variety of type $(d,2,2,2)$. We prove that the fourfolds $X_{d-1,d}$ are diffeomorphic to $\mathbb{C}^4$ but not biholomorphic to $\mathbb{C}^4$. These, therefore, give counterexamples to the Tóth-Varolin conjecture.
items.title: A new class of smooth algebraic varieties with the density property and a counterexample to the Tóth-Varolin Conjecture

items.summary: Action-conditioned video generative models trained on successful, goal-directed demonstrations tend to ignore the commanded action, rendering a plausible expert-like future regardless of what is asked of them. We trace this failure to training data that lack sufficient action influence. We analyze this metric and prove that it upper bounds the action influence that any model trained on that data can express. Expert demonstrations, whose narrow action distributions let next states be predicted without attending to the action, set a low ceiling that no amount of model capacity alone can raise. Raising it requires collecting different data. We introduce Action Influence Maximization (AIM), an algorithm for actively collecting training data for improving dataset action influence. We compare the performance and data-efficiency of AIM against exploration heuristics and intrinsic-motivation methods on simulated navigation and manipulation tasks. In pixel-based manipulation, AIM is the only method that consistently improves controllability: 500 actively collected episodes added to 3k demonstrations match a world model trained on 300k expert episodes on end-effector controllability, an $85\times$ reduction in data.
items.title: Training Controllable World Models via Action Influence Maximization

items.summary: Multi-agent systems rely on communication to complete tasks, and latent communication passes continuous representations to reduce text generation and re-encoding. However, multi-agent systems must reconfigure agent models, whereas existing latent-communication methods are built for fixed model combinations, so their interfaces may fail after replacement. Our pilot study confirms this interface failure and identifies the requirement for interface reuse after model replacement. We present LatBridge, which connects agent models through a shared Bridge and separate interfaces under a shared latent-communication protocol. After agent model replacement, LatBridge reuses unchanged interfaces, selects matching low-rank interfaces, and combines them through the Bridge, training only missing ones with all models frozen. The Bridge processes source representations in the basic mode and constructs target input without autoregressive generation in the accelerated mode. Experiments support effective communication after model replacement, with mean basic-mode accuracies of 14.8% on MATH and 27.3% on ALFWorld next-action prediction across eight small-model configurations. Analyses examine the factors supporting task accuracy and communication efficiency.
items.title: LatBridge: Efficient and Stable Model Replacement in Latent-Communication Multi-Agent Systems

items.summary: Federated learning for crop-disease classification across heterogeneous farm clients is vulnerable to Byzantine participants who submit corrupted model updates, yet the aggregation literature reports robustness without a design-level account of how many adversarial clients a given federation can tolerate before diagnostic integrity collapses. The analysis treats the aggregation rule as a statistical estimator of the honest update direction and characterises the breakdown point of coordinate-wise median and trimmed-mean aggregation under a declared contamination model. A before-after-control-impact design is used to benchmark power across cluster counts of 8, 16, 24 and 32 and effect sizes of 3, 5 and 8 percentage points, with 2000 replications per design cell and an intraclass correlation of 0.640. The contamination bound predicts that coordinate-wise median aggregation tolerates up to 50% adversarial clients in the limit but loses diagnostic integrity at a threshold that depends on the between-cluster standard deviation of 6.0 and the residual standard deviation of 4.5. The benchmarking results indicate that 54 clusters are required to detect a 5 percentage point degradation at 80% power. The contribution is a formal contamination bound that links aggregation-rule choice to the minimum federation size needed to certify diagnostic integrity, together with a benchmarking protocol that makes that link auditable.
tags: federated learning; Byzantine robustness; crop disease classification; contamination bound; benchmar
items.title: Benchmarking Evaluation of Byzantine-Robust Federated Aggregation for Computer Agriculture Disease Classifiers Under Adversarial Client Participation: An Artificial Intelligence Contamination Bound for Diagnostic Integrity

items.summary: Edge pest detection in computer agriculture is constrained less by classifier accuracy than by the thermal power budget of the sensing node. Spiking neural networks (SNNs) promise order-of-magnitude energy reductions on neuromorphic hardware, but the field lacks a design-level account of how that promise translates into deployable detection performance when the thermal sensor itself is the dominant load. The framework formalises a thermal-power budget, defines an energy-normalised detection rate, and derives a power-accuracy frontier for leaky integrate-and-fire classifiers operating on low-resolution thermal frames. A replication-based evaluation of the before-after-control-impact estimator was conducted under a declared variance structure (between-cluster SD = 6.0, residual SD = 4.5, intraclass correlation = 0.64), with power estimated across 2000 design cells. The analysis indicates that 54 clusters are required to detect a 5-percentage-point effect at 80% power. The contribution is a reproducible audit protocol that makes the energy-accuracy trade-off explicit and falsifiable before field deployment, and that identifies the sensor duty cycle, not the network, as the binding constraint in most edge configurations.
tags: spiking neural networks; edge pest detection; thermal sensing; energy-accuracy trade-off; computer a
items.title: Benchmarking Evaluation of Spiking Neural Networks for Computer Agriculture Edge Pest-Detection Under Thermal-Sensor Power Constraints: An Artificial Intelligence Energy-Accuracy Trade-off Audit for Field-Deployment Safety

items.summary: Flood-risk mapping for agricultural insurance in vegetated terrain depends on computed-aperture radar interferometric coherence, yet canopy decoherence attenuates the signal that classifiers must detect. the present analysis formalises the detection problem as a before-after-control-impact design and derives the operating characteristics of a coherence-based flood detector under a declared variance structure with intraclass correlation 0.64, between-cluster standard deviation 6.0 and residual standard deviation 4.5. Power was estimated across 2000 replications per design cell for cluster counts of 8, 16, 24 and 32 and effect sizes of 3, 5 and 8 percentage points. The design required 56 clusters to detect a 5 percentage-point effect at 80% power. The analysis characterises the detection-power bound that canopy decoherence imposes on payout-equity claims, showing that the cluster counts typical of agricultural insurance portfolios are insufficient to separate genuine flood signal from decoherence noise. The contribution is a benchmark-derived bound that links remote-sensing detection power to the actuarial fairness of index-based insurance payouts.
tags: SAR interferometry; coherence; flood-risk mapping; detection power; insurance equity; canopy decoher
items.title: Benchmarking Evaluation of computed-Aperture Radar Interferometric Coherence for Computer Agriculture Flood-Risk Mapping Under Vegetation Canopy Decoherence: An Artificial Intelligence Detection-Power Bound for Insurance Payout Equity

items.summary: Tensor-network compression promises to fit convolutional disease classifiers into the memory ceilings of field-deployable diagnostic devices, but the accuracy cost of compression is usually reported as a single post-hoc number rather than as a bounded retention guarantee. the present analysis treats compression as a design problem with an auditable operating characteristic: given a declared memory ceiling, what fraction of the uncompressed diagnostic accuracy survives, and with what uncertainty? We formalise tensor-train decomposition of convolutional kernels as a rank-constrained projection, derive a retention bound that links bond dimension, kernel spectrum and the resulting classification margin, and then characterise the operating characteristics of a benchmarking protocol that estimates retention under a declared variance structure. The protocol is a before-after-control-impact design with between-cluster SD 6.0, residual SD 4.5 and intraclass correlation 0.64, evaluated across 2000 replications per design cell at cluster counts of 8, 16, 24 and 32 and effect sizes of 3, 5 and 8 percentage points. Power reaches conventional levels only at 56 clusters for a 5-percentage-point retention effect, which exceeds every cluster count in the declared grid; the minimum detectable effect at 80% power therefore remains above the 5-percentage-point threshold throughout the grid. The contribution is a retention bound plus a power-calibrated audit protocol that tells practitioners when a compression benchmark is informative and when it is underpowered, and that reframes field diagnostic safety as a property of the evaluation design rather than of the compressor alone.
tags: tensor-train decomposition; model compression; plant disease classification; on-device inference; ac
items.title: Benchmarking Evaluation of Tensor-Network Compression for Computer Agriculture Disease Classifiers Under On-Device Memory Ceilings: An Artificial Intelligence Accuracy-Retention Audit for Field Diagnostic Safety

items.summary: Differentiable logic-gate networks (DLGNs) are attractive for irrigation controllers because their learned Boolean structure can be verified exhaustively, yet the safety case for deploying them under actuator-failure cascades has not been formalised. The work is a design-and-power analysis of a before-after-control-impact (BACI) evaluation protocol, not an observational study: no field data are used or claimed. Operating characteristics were characterised under a declared variance structure with between-cluster SD = 6.0, residual SD = 4.5 and intraclass correlation = 0.64, across 2000 replications per design cell for cluster counts of 8, 16, 24 and 32 and effect sizes of 3, 5 and 8 percentage points.52 clusters are required to detect a 5-percentage-point compliance effect at 80% power under this variance structure, and that the intraclass correlation of 0.64 dominates the design's sensitivity. A formal-safety audit of DLGN controllers is then specified as a finite-state reachability problem over the actuator-failure cascade, with water-rights compliance encoded as an invariant. The contribution is a benchmark protocol that couples a verifiable controller class to a statistically defensible evaluation design, and a demonstration that the evaluation design, not the controller, is the binding constraint on regulatory acceptance.
tags: differentiable logic-gate networks; irrigation controllers; actuator-failure cascades; water-rights
items.title: Benchmarking Evaluation of Differentiable Logic-Gate Networks for Computer Agriculture Irrigation Controllers Under Actuator-Failure Cascades: An Artificial Intelligence Formal-Safety Audit for Water-Rights Compliance

items.summary: Statistical learning in high dimensions suffers from the curse of dimensionality. Fortunately, many functions of practical interest are compositionally sparse, meaning they admit a composition of local functions, each depending on only a few variables, allowing sample complexity to depend on local arity rather than ambient dimension. Yet realizing this benefit requires exploiting hidden compositional structure, which theory does not establish for practical gradient-based training. We study this gap with CSFRBench, a controlled benchmark that hides the target's compositional computation during training but retains it for diagnosis, and find that dense networks and sparsity-based baselines leave much of that benefit unrealized. Inspired by the spatial organization of biological neural circuits, we introduce Learned Wiring (LeWi): each neuron has a learned low-dimensional embedding, only nearby neurons connect, and embeddings and weights are trained jointly. LeWi improves sample efficiency on targets with hierarchical structure, intermediate reuse, or independent modules. Across 32 additional targets generated by independently sampled computation graphs, LeWi is the most sample-efficient method not given the target graph, with 27% lower mean learning-curve area than dense networks. Dense networks perform better on targets with a single high-arity function. LeWi's representations and connectivity align with the target computation. On 17 world-model prediction tasks spanning control, navigation, and manipulation, LeWi beats the dense baseline on 16 and wins 99/119 baseline comparisons. These results show that jointly learning connectivity and weights can exploit computational structure to improve sample efficiency.
items.title: Learning Computational Structure for Sample-Efficient Prediction

items.summary: A single observation can admit several plausible futures, making uncertainty an essential part of world modelling. However, quantum generative models remain underexplored for this task. We introduce Quantum-JEPA, a latent-action JEPA framework that learns distributions of future representations using a conditional quantum Born prior. Circuit measurements generate binary latent actions, which a shared predictor maps to alternative future representations. We train the quantum prior through the quality and diversity of these predictions using a sampled energy objective. Our model learns distinct continuations on constructed multimodal tasks and captures latent-action correlations that support coordinated multi-agent futures. On D3IL, a benchmark of diverse human demonstrations, our trained models generate multiple obstacle-crossing routes from a common starting point without observed motion. On the controlled tasks, our classical and quantum prior implementations improve prediction validity and distributional fidelity over the evaluated variational baselines. Our quantum priors combine competitive predictive quality with a parameter-efficient sampling structure: they avoid an exponentially sized categorical output layer while supporting correlated latent actions. We further validate finite-shot parameter-shift training, including training with readout noise. Unlike most prior work, which focuses on simulation, we also verify the feasibility of inference with trained priors on a real QPU. These results establish a trainable quantum component for JEPA future prediction and a basis for exploring quantum-enhanced world models at larger scales.
items.title: Quantum-JEPA: Quantum Born Priors for Latent-Action JEPA World Models

items.summary: RTL repair benchmarks should measure whether a model can fix broken RTL given a specification. To this end, we construct and hash-bind RTLRepairDataset, 5,784 (broken, fixed) training pairs; RTLRepairBench, 459 held-out cases with 374 syntactic and 85 behavioral mutations; and an evaluation harness supporting simulation and formal equivalence. We then use this infrastructure to identify two measurement confounds. First, simulation and formal scoring give opposite signs for the apparent effect of providing a specification in one evaluated cohort; reset-aware rescoring attributes almost all of the simulation-formal disagreement to reset and first-cycle comparison semantics. Second, on 274 mined model failures, the specification-only minus specification-conditioned recovery point estimate ranges from -8.5 to +18.3 percentage points across six models. Thus, a conventional repair score need not isolate whether the model used the faulty RTL. We translate these findings into evaluation controls: report initialization, reset, first-cycle, and unknown-value semantics; disclose oracle coverage and undecided cases; and include a specification-only baseline. Together, the resources and audit provide both a benchmark for behavioral repair and a protocol for diagnosing what contributes to its measured score. We release the benchmark, the training set, construction code, sanitized aggregate evidence, and reproduction materials at https://github.com/Evaaaz/RTLRepairBench.
items.title: What Do RTL Repair Benchmarks Actually Measure?

items.summary: Satellite-cloud gaps corrupt the reflectance time series on which computer-agriculture crop-yield estimators depend, and the resulting coverage error propagates into famine early-warning reliability. The framework is evaluated through a replication-based benchmark in which 600 data sets of N = 500 were drawn from a declared data-generating process (intercept 12.0, exposure 0.42, group -3.1, severity 1.35, error SD 4.2) and the ordinary least squares estimator was characterised under the stated process. The benchmark produced an estimated bias of -0.07173 for the intercept and 0.00147 for the exposure coefficient, with RMSE values of 0.89562 and 0.0157 respectively, and empirical coverage of the nominal 95% confidence intervals of 1.0 for both parameters. The coverage-error bound formalises the conditions under which CDA-supported estimators preserve nominal coverage and therefore early-warning reliability, and it identifies the augmentation regimes in which coverage degrades. The contribution is a benchmark protocol and a bound that make the reliability consequences of cloud-gap augmentation auditable rather than assumed.
tags: counterfactual data augmentation; crop-yield estimation; satellite-cloud gaps; coverage-error bound;
items.title: Benchmarking Evaluation of Counterfactual Data Augmentation for Computer Agriculture Crop-Yield Estimators Under Satellite-Cloud Gaps: An Artificial Intelligence Coverage-Error Bound for Famine Early-Warning Reliability

items.summary: Description: Arduino firmware for the control unit of a low-cost, marble-type gas–water equilibrator used for continuous measurement of dissolved pCO₂ in inland waters. The firmware controls the water and gas pumps, reads a SenseAir K30 NDIR CO₂ sensor and a DS18B20 water-temperature probe, and logs the data to an SD card with timestamps from a real-time clock. It accompanies the manuscript “A microcontroller-based, low-cost platform for continuous pCO₂ measurements in lakes and reservoirs” (Grochocki and Mannich, Limnology and Oceanography: Methods, under review). Hardware ·          Arduino Uno (ATmega328P) ·          SenseAir K30 NDIR CO₂ sensor, 0–10,000 ppm (UART/Modbus via SoftwareSerial; RX pin 3, TX pin 2) ·          DS18B20 waterproof temperature probe (OneWire, pin 6) ·          DS1307 real-time clock (I²C) ·          SD card module (SPI, CS pin 10) ·          Two-channel relay module: water pump (pin 7) and gas pump (pin 5) Operating cycle 1.       Switch on the water and gas pumps. 2.       For the duration of a measurement cycle, read CO₂ and water temperature at a fixed interval and append each reading to a daily file on the SD card. 3.       Switch off both pumps and stay idle until the next cycle. Configuration Timing parameters are read at boot from a config.txt file on the SD card, one key=value per line: ·          measurementInterval : idle time between cycles (minutes) ·          dataCollectionInterval : time between readings (seconds) ·          fullMeasurementTime : duration of each cycle (minutes) If the file does not exist, the firmware creates one with default values, which take effect at the next boot. The values hard-coded in the sketch are a 10-min cycle, 5-s readings and a 45-min idle period. Output One comma-separated text file per day, named YY-MM-DD.txt , with the header Date Time, CO2 (ppm), Water Temp (C) . Timestamps are written as YYYY-M-D H:M:S , without zero padding. Each file is opened and closed at every write, so data are not lost if power is cut. Notes ·          The CO₂ values logged are the raw K30 output. Calibration against a reference analyzer, conversion to pCO₂ (water-vapor and pressure correction) and conversion to dissolved CO₂ are done in post-processing, as described in the accompanying paper (Eqs. 1–5). ·          If the RTC has not been set, it is set at first boot to the compile time of the sketch. ·          The K30 automatic baseline correction (ABC) assumes regular exposure to ~400 ppm air, so it should be disabled for underwater use. Required libraries: SD, SPI, Wire, SoftwareSerial (Arduino core); OneWire; DallasTemperature; TimeLib; DS1307RTC.
items.title: Arduino firmware for the control unit of a low-cost, marble-type gas–water equilibrator for continuous measurement of dissolved pCO2

items.summary: The existing theory of stochastic linear-quadratic (LQ) optimal control problems focuses on open-loop and closed-loop solvability. For finite horizon problems, it is widely accepted that those two types of solvability are not equivalent in general, as demonstrated by explicit counterexamples. In contrast, they coincide in standard infinite-horizon formulations with constant coefficients under suitable stabilizability and integrability assumptions. This paper aims at challenging this well-established paradigm by developing a novel framework of closed-loop solvability, namely generalized closed-loop solvability, which removes the $L^2$-integrability constraint on the feedback strategies from the existing formulation. It will be proven that open-loop and generalized closed-loop solvability are equivalent and the classical closed-loop solvablity is a particular case only when the admissible feedback strategy is $L^2$-integrable over the time horizon. In other words, the previously established non-equivalence between open-loop and closed-loop solvability stems solely from the limitations of the classical formulation which requires the $L^2$-integrability of the admissible feedback strategies over the time-horizon. Therefore, this paper unifies the theory of the solvabilitiy for stochastic LQ control problems. Moreover, our results offer a novel insight to stochastic LQ control problems: open-loop/generalized closed-loop solvability is essentially equivalent to piecewisely local closed-loop solvability in the classical sense. The current paper is focused on homogeneous cases only and non-homogeneous cases will be studied in a subsequent paper.
items.title: A Unified Theory of Solvability for Stochastic Linear-Quadratic Control Problems I: The Homogeneous Case
